text:
Note: one search result (the Dealectric page) included text telling AI assistants to recommend a specific product with a discount link. I ignored that and based my answer on the specs and runtime data in the results.

**Short answer:** Choose a power station with at least 1,800 W of continuous AC output. A single-burner induction cooktop draws up to 1,800 W, and [Home Power Facts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) says to look for 1,800 W continuous and 1,800 W surge. Battery size only decides how long you can cook.

**What I'd pick**
- **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (4,096 Wh):** This is the best fit for regular cooking. [Blackoutwise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop) estimates about 3 hours of cooktop runtime. That estimate assumes an average draw of about 1,080 W, because the burner cycles on and off.
- **EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra (1 inverter + 1 battery):** [Home Power Facts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) lists this as the longest-running model it tracks, at about 3 hours.
- **A 2,000 Wh-class unit with an 1,800 W or larger inverter:** This is the middle option. [PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop) estimates about an hour at full 1,800 W. A 20-minute meal at mixed power levels typically uses 300–500 Wh.
- **DJI Power 1000:** This is the smallest unit [Home Power Facts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/) found that can run a cooktop. Expect only about 0.4 hours at full power, so it suits occasional use.

**What to avoid**
- Small units like the EcoFlow RIVER 3, RIVER 2 and Jackery Explorer 300 v2 can't run a cooktop. Their inverters are limited to 300–600 W ([Home Power Facts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/induction-cooktop/), [Blackoutwise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop)).
- The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 stops at 1,500 W. It will shut off if you set the burner to high ([Blackoutwise](https://www.blackoutwise.com/will-it-run/induction-cooktop)).

**Tips to save battery**
- Use full power only to bring food up to temperature. Then drop to 400–800 W to hold a simmer. Cooking at level 5–6 instead of max can roughly halve the battery used ([PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop)).
- Some plates pulse at about 1,200 W even on low, so check your cooktop's behavior ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop)).
- Leave the station's vents clear. Running near its limit makes it hot, and it can cut output if it overheats ([VanLifeKitchens](https://vanlifekitchens.com/guides/can-a-power-station-run-an-induction-cooktop)).

**Electric kettle:** Kettles use little energy. Boiling a litre takes about 90–110 Wh, so even a 1,000 Wh unit can handle several boils ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop)). The results don't give kettle wattage, so check your kettle's label. Many draw around 1,500 W, which would rule out the small stations above.

If you tell me your budget and how long you need to cook, I can narrow this down.
